source.title: Quantization Methods for Energy Efficient LLM Deployments

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares downstream benchmark performance across model sizes, a different measurement from held-out cross-entropy scaling, and reports results bearing on V6. It does not fit or test the pretraining-loss or compute-optimal laws.
record.gate_note: The benchmark results across sizes bear on V6. The Metabench quantization-retention results are recorded as findings about scaling-related quantization resilience, which none of the versions specifies. Energy and throughput results do not measure the claim versions. The paper cites Chinchilla scaling laws as background, but those cited results are not this study's own results.
record.test_reason: This is a post-training quantization study of Qwen3 (0.6B–32B). Its own results concern accuracy retention after quantization, plus energy and throughput. None of these is pretraining loss, compute allocation, or downstream performance as a function of scale. Section 4.1 describes quantization error shrinking with size, not FP16 benchmark scores rising with size. Chinchilla is cited only as background on OPT being undertrained. The Figure 1 benchmark-by-size curves might bear on V6, but the text reports no FP16 scaling trend from them.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but should be sharpened. The authors find no clear overall scaling pattern in quantization resilience in Section 4.1, yet conclude larger models are more resilient 'in most cases'. They also conclude that FP8/INT8 W8A8 give the best energy and throughput gains: about 2x, with a 32B FP8 model using energy comparable to an 8B FP16 model.
record.recipe_differences: This is an inference-time quantization and benchmark study, not a held-out pretraining-loss scaling-law fit or compute-allocation experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Benchmark outcomes and reported quantization resilience differ by quantization method and model size.

fits_no_version.finding: MetaBench retention after quantization (Table 1) rises with size for AWQ (90.07%→98.28%), GPTQ-4bit and FP8, but not consistently for GPTQ-8bit and INT8. Section 4.1 says quantization error on MMLU, ARC and WinoGrande shrinks with size, while TruthfulQA retention depends more on method than on scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness to post-training quantization increases with model size, depending on the quantization method and benchmark.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on AI Research (ICAIR 2025)
record.problems: Figure 1 is not numerically tabulated in the supplied text, and its benchmark trends are described qualitatively. The study covers only the Qwen3 family and does not report uncertainty for the benchmark results.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured or fitted.
No compute-optimal allocation tested; Chinchilla is only cited.
No shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime tested.
FP16 downstream performance versus model size is plotted in Figure 1 but not reported or analysed in the text. There is no relation to pretraining loss.
No exponents or fitting choices analysed.

missing.what: FP16 baseline benchmark scores by model size (0.6B–32B), which would bear on V6 if digitised. The text gives no numbers, and its HumanEval/GSM8K remarks hint at a non-monotonic FP16 trend.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked R1–R6 to V6 by reading descriptions of quantization error as descriptions of downstream scaling. I reassigned them to none and filed them under the quantization-resilience construct. The study is a quantization and deployment paper whose only link to scaling laws is a Chinchilla citation, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute is not measured.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run held-out loss.
No fixed-compute training allocation or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
The paper does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No power-law test in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer is reported.
The paper evaluates downstream benchmarks across model sizes, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit a quantitative downstream-versus-scale relation.
No exponents, fitting choices, compute-optimal splits, or bends in fitted loss curves are analyzed.

rows.subject: Qwen3 model family (0.6B–32B)
rows.operation_detail: Benchmark performance compared across model sizes and quantization methods.
rows.value: figure only; text says errors reduce and stabilize as model size scales across MMLU, ARC Challenge, and WinoGrande.
rows.note: The paper gives a shared qualitative description for these language-understanding benchmarks; it does not state separate numerical MMLU values in the text.
rows.check: The quoted text ('consistent errors which reduce and stabilise as we scale') describes quantization error versus FP16, not downstream performance improving with scale. It measures quantization resilience, so it is not a V6 row. Figure 1 values are not readable from the text.

rows.value: figure only; text says errors reduce and stabilize as model size scales across MMLU, ARC Challenge, and WinoGrande.
rows.note: The paper gives a shared qualitative description for these language-understanding benchmarks; it does not state separate numerical ARC Challenge values in the text.
rows.check: Same as R1: it measures quantization-error behaviour across sizes, not V6 downstream scaling. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: Qwen3 model family (0.6B–32B)
rows.operation_detail: Benchmark performance compared across model sizes and quantization methods.
rows.value: figure only; text says errors reduce and stabilize as model size scales across MMLU, ARC Challenge, and WinoGrande.
rows.note: The paper gives a shared qualitative description for these language-understanding benchmarks; it does not state separate numerical WinoGrande values in the text.
rows.check: Same as R1. WinoGrande also appears in Figure 1 and Section 4.1 but is not in the stated benchmark list; values are figure-only.

rows.subject: Qwen3 model family (0.6B–32B)
rows.operation_detail: Benchmark performance compared across model sizes and quantization methods.
rows.value: figure only; text says smaller models have pronounced degradation, larger models—especially Qwen3-14B—show large discrepancies between quantization methods, and AWQ can perform significantly better than the FP16 baseline.
rows.note: The textual summary emphasizes differences by size and quantization method rather than a single predictable improvement with scale.
rows.check: The text describes method-dependent quantization discrepancies, including AWQ beating FP16 at 14B, not FP16 performance versus scale. The 'partial' state for V6 is unsupported.

rows.subject: Qwen3 model family (0.6B–32B)
rows.operation_detail: Benchmark performance compared across model sizes and quantization methods.
rows.value: figure only; text says the scaling performance is similar to GSM8K, coding and mathematical abilities may degrade even without quantization, and GPTQ-8bit and AWQ can outperform FP16.
rows.note: The paper reports method-dependent differences and does not state a quantitative downstream scaling relation.
rows.check: The text describes quantization-method effects relative to FP16. 'Degrades even without quantization' is too vague to give an FP16 trend with size. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: Qwen3 model family (0.6B–32B)
rows.operation_detail: Benchmark performance compared across model sizes and quantization methods.
rows.value: figure only; text says factual accuracy shows consistent degradation patterns across model sizes and is more dependent on quantization method than model scale.
rows.note: The described dependence on quantization method limits a general scale-based predictability claim.
rows.check: The text says retention depends more on quantization method than on scale, which is a quantization-resilience finding, not V6. Values are figure-only.
